title: Union benefits, scale and refusing low pay
summary: Early benefits were a $250 death payment; scale meant turning down work, but as membership grew musicians gained bargaining power.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: At the time you joined what were union benefits? What would it do for you, particularly?

Well, I think, if I'm not mistaken, I think you only go -- I think it was $250.00. That was, you know, your death benefit. That's what you got out of it, $250.00. And of course the dues, I don't remember what the dues were at that time, but it wasn't very much, you know. And this is -- you know, naturally, if you were sick you got a little help from the union, but they didn't have any money to really do too much for you. But the union was important, you know, it was important to you. It helped -- it did help us to better meet our obligations, to get more money, to earn more money, you know, put you in a better earning position.
If you were a union member you had to get whatever union scale was.
Did it ever put you in the position of having to turn down work because an employer wouldn't pay union scale?
Well, that's true, yes, oh, yes. Yes. Even as little as it was then, there were some people who they

were so used to not, you know, they were so used to paying a little $2.00 a night, or whatever. That's all I was getting when I first worked, when I came here, as I told you, at the Dunbar Hotel. I was getting -- for six hours work I got $2.00 a night. But I made tips, you know, and the tips, of course, that helped an awful lot because people were good tippers, and many of the clubs, many of the better clubs didn't pay -- they didn't pay much more than that.
Did it take a while to get employers educated?

Well, yes. They got -- well, it's like anything else, this is the purpose of a union. As the union grew, the membership grew, naturally the union became strengthened and with people saying, "No, I can't afford to work for that kind of money. I can't work for that." You know, even though it hurt, because you needed, you know, you needed the money.

So, as the union -- as the membership, rather, grew, then you know, we got in a bargaining position. We got to the place where we could really make a living and a fairly decent living, according to the times, according to what you were paying, 15.00 and $20.00 a month rent. Can you imagine that? I can hardly believe that ever happened.
